planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this older Dutch-bred cultivar grows tall and benefits from generous spacing and good air movement to limit the powdery mildew that affects most Monarda didyma selections by late summer.

directions: Prairienacht (Dutch for 'Prairie Night') is a long-cultivated European selection of bee balm valued for its deep violet-purple flower heads, a richer, cooler tone than the scarlet-red typical of most older didyma cultivars. It forms an upright, clump-forming stand well suited to the middle or back of a perennial border, where its dark blooms read well against silver or chartreuse foliage companions. Like other tall bee balms, it draws hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies over a long midsummer bloom season and spreads gradually by rhizome, so divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor and airflow through the planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; this English heirloom cultivar shows its distinctive bract coloring best where nights stay cool and humidity is moderate, so prioritize sites with open air circulation.

directions: Beauty of Cobham is a vintage English bee balm selection prized for its soft, pale pink petals set off by dusky purple-mauve bracts and stems, a subtler color combination than the scarlets and magentas of most Monarda didyma cultivars. The contrast between the pale flowers and dark calyces gives the plant a two-toned effect that reads well in cottage-garden and cutting-garden plantings alike. It shares the species' appetite for consistent moisture and its susceptibility to powdery mildew in still, humid air, so thin stems in spring and avoid overhead watering late in the day. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the flowers freely through the midsummer bloom period.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this older German-bred cultivar reblooms reliably if deadheaded and benefits from division every few years to keep clumps vigorous and airy.

directions: Adam is a long-established German heirloom bee balm carrying dense, shaggy heads of rosy cherry-red flowers on a somewhat more compact frame than tall scarlet cultivars like Cambridge Scarlet. Its dependable color and steady rebloom after deadheading have kept it in circulation in perennial borders for decades, even as newer mildew-resistant introductions have crowded the market. Give it full sun, even moisture, and room for air to move between clumps, since crowded, humid conditions bring on powdery mildew more readily in this older selection than in modern resistant hybrids. Hummingbirds and bumblebees are frequent visitors through its midsummer bloom window.
